document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped taking her anticoagulant two weeks ago presents with 4 hours of sudden severe right leg pain. The right leg is cold and pale, and femoral, popliteal and pedal pulses are absent. Sensation and motor power in the foot are intact and arterial Doppler signals are audible at the ankle. Which of the following is the best initial management?

options.text: Weight-based intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus followed by continuous infusion
Emergency four-compartment fasciotomy of the calf
Primary above-knee amputation
Oral anticoagulation alone with elective vascular clinic follow-up
Graduated compression stockings and analgesia

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists immediate unfractionated heparinization with a weight-based bolus and continuous infusion titrated to PTT as the first treatment step in acute limb ischemia, together with IV fluids, urine output monitoring, analgesia and supplemental oxygen. Because her neurovascular status is intact there may be time for further workup including CTA, but anticoagulation should not wait for imaging.

optionExplanations.b: Fasciotomy is used for compartment syndrome secondary to reperfusion after prolonged ischemia, not as the initial step before revascularization.
optionExplanations.c: Primary amputation or palliation is reserved for irreversible ischemia (Rutherford category III) with profound anesthesia and paralysis.
optionExplanations.d: Oral anticoagulation is started postoperatively once the patient is stable; it is too slow for an acutely threatened limb.
optionExplanations.e: Compression and analgesia do not address arterial occlusion and skeletal muscle tolerates only about 6 hours of total ischemia.

questions.question: A 69-year-old man who stopped smoking 5 years ago is found on a screening ultrasound to have a 4.4 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. He is asymptomatic, the abdomen is non-tender with no pain on palpation of the aneurysm, and the aneurysm is fusiform. Blood pressure is 148/88 mmHg and he takes no lipid-lowering therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Open surgical repair now
Endovascular aneurysm repair now
Cardiovascular risk factor modification with ultrasound surveillance
Urgent CT angiography and emergency repair
Discharge with no further aortic follow-up

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes reserves conservative management for asymptomatic aneurysms that do not meet the size threshold for repair, consisting of cardiovascular risk factor reduction (smoking cessation, control of hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia including statins, regular exercise) plus ultrasound surveillance at a frequency determined by size and location. Surgical indications are rupture, symptoms, an AAA above 5.5 cm in men or 5.0 cm in women, rapid growth, saccular morphology, pseudoaneurysm or mycotic aneurysm; this fusiform asymptomatic 4.4 cm aneurysm meets none of these.

optionExplanations.a: Open repair carries an operative mortality of 2-5% and is not justified below the size threshold in an asymptomatic patient.
optionExplanations.b: EVAR is an alternative repair technique but the indication for any repair has not been met.
optionExplanations.d: Emergency imaging and repair apply to rupture or symptomatic aneurysm, neither of which is present.
optionExplanations.e: Abandoning follow-up is unsafe because surveillance ultrasound is required to detect growth toward the repair threshold.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes reports right calf pain that comes on reproducibly after walking two blocks and resolves within 3 minutes of standing rest. The skin over the shin is shiny with hair loss and pedal pulses are difficult to palpate. Ankle-brachial index measures 1.42 on the right and 1.38 on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Toe-brachial index study
Accept the ankle-brachial index as normal and stop the vascular workup
MRI of the lumbar spine
Invasive catheter arteriography
Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the lower limbs

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that ABI values above 1.3 suggest non-compressible heavily calcified arteries, which are common in diabetes and produce falsely elevated readings. It recommends ABI and/or a TBI study to confirm the diagnosis of PAD, and specifically identifies toe pressure and TBI as useful in patients with non-compressible vessels. His history of reproducible exertional calf pain relieved by short rest is classic vascular claudication, so the workup must continue with a TBI.

optionExplanations.b: An index above 1.30 indicates a non-compressible vessel rather than a normal study, so it cannot be used to exclude PAD.
optionExplanations.c: Neurospinal disease is in the differential of leg pain, but pain reproducible at a fixed distance and relieved by short rest without postural change is vascular claudication.
optionExplanations.d: Arteriography is invasive and is used for superior resolution or as part of an intervention, not to confirm a diagnosis of PAD at the bedside.
optionExplanations.e: CTA is used primarily for planning interventions and carries contrast-induced nephropathy risk; confirmation of PAD comes first from ABI/TBI.

questions.question: A 71-year-old man had a 20-minute episode of right arm weakness and difficulty producing speech 3 days ago and has since fully recovered. Carotid duplex ultrasound shows 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. He has hypertension and dyslipidemia, is an acceptable operative candidate with normal neck anatomy, and has never had neck irradiation. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Best medical therapy alone with no revascularization
Best medical therapy plus carotid endarterectomy within the next 2 weeks
Best medical therapy plus carotid artery angioplasty and stenting
Best medical therapy now with reassessment for surgery in 6 months
Warfarin anticoagulation in place of antiplatelet therapy

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines symptomatic carotid stenosis as focal neurologic deficits referable to the carotid distribution within the past 6 months with greater than 50% stenosis, and states that surgical treatment should ideally be done within the first 48 hours to 2 weeks of symptom onset. Carotid endarterectomy is described as generally the mainstay of treatment, given alongside best medical therapy including antihypertensives, statins, antiplatelet agents and smoking cessation.

optionExplanations.a: Medical therapy alone leaves a high-grade symptomatic lesion untreated when the patient is a suitable surgical candidate.
optionExplanations.c: Stenting is indicated for poor surgical access, radiation-induced stenosis or comorbidities that increase operative risk, none of which apply, and it carries a higher periprocedural stroke risk.
optionExplanations.d: Delaying by 6 months forfeits the recommended 48-hour to 2-week window after symptom onset.
optionExplanations.e: Antiplatelet therapy with ASA and clopidogrel is the described medical regimen for carotid disease; substituting warfarin is not supported.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman with obesity and a prior deep vein thrombosis has a shallow, weeping ulcer with irregular edges just above the medial malleolus. The surrounding skin shows brown hyperpigmentation and eczema, and there is ankle and calf edema that improves with elevation. The ulcer causes little pain. The plan is to begin multilayer compression bandaging with wound care. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation before compression is applied?

options.text: Ankle-brachial index
Wound swab for culture and sensitivity
Lymphoscintigraphy
Punch biopsy of the ulcer edge
CT venography of the pelvis

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists the investigations for chronic venous insufficiency as ankle-brachial index, performed pre-compression to ensure there is no arterial disease, together with venous Doppler or duplex ultrasound. The described ulcer above the medial malleolus that is shallow, weeping, painless and irregularly edged, with hemosiderin pigmentation, eczema and elevation-responsive edema, is a venous ulcer, and compression bandaging is the conservative treatment, but occult arterial disease must be excluded first.

optionExplanations.b: Antibiotics are used as part of ulcer care when indicated, but a swab does not determine whether compression is safe to apply.
optionExplanations.c: Lymphoscintigraphy is the definitive test for lymphedema, which causes non-pitting edema and a positive Stemmer sign rather than a weeping gaiter-area ulcer.
optionExplanations.d: Biopsy is not part of the described workup for chronic venous insufficiency.
optionExplanations.e: Pelvic venous imaging is not listed among the investigations for chronic venous insufficiency and does not address arterial safety.

source.reference: VS11 — Chronic Venous Insufficiency, Investigations and Treatment

questions.question: A 78-year-old man develops abrupt severe left foot pain while sitting watching television and can state the exact minute it began. He has never had exertional calf pain and has had no previous vascular surgery or stenting. He has atrial fibrillation and admits to missing several doses of his anticoagulant. The left foot is cold and pulseless, while pulses and Doppler signals in the right leg are normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?

options.text: Arterial embolism from a cardiac source
In-situ thrombosis of a high-grade atherosclerotic plaque
Occlusion of a previously placed bypass graft
Traumatic arterial dissection of a lower limb vessel
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes identifies cardiogenic embolism as the most common cause of acute limb ischemia and lists the features that should raise suspicion of embolism: acute onset that the patient can recall precisely, a history of embolism, a known embolic source such as a cardiac arrhythmia or a lapse in prescribed anticoagulation, no prior intermittent claudication or arterial intervention, and normal pulses or Doppler signals in the unaffected limb. This man has every one of those features.

optionExplanations.b: In-situ thrombosis is suspected with a prior history of intermittent claudication and an abnormal pulse examination in the unaffected limb, neither of which is present.
optionExplanations.c: Graft or stent occlusion is the most common cause of arterial thrombosis after previous reconstruction, but he has had no vascular intervention.
optionExplanations.d: Isolated arterial dissection of vessels supplying the lower limbs is uncommon and arises from trauma or collagen disorders, with no such history here.
optionExplanations.e: HITT is a hypercoagulable cause of acute limb ischemia but requires heparin exposure and would be suggested by thrombocytopenia.

source.reference: VS3 — Acute Limb Ischemia, Etiology (Embolism vs Thrombosis)

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension develops sudden onset tearing chest pain radiating between the scapulae. Blood pressure is 196/104 mmHg, heart rate 98 bpm. There is no diastolic murmur, and abdominal, limb and neurologic examinations are normal. CTA shows a Type B aortic dissection with no spinal, mesenteric or limb malperfusion. He is admitted to the critical care unit. Which of the following is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion
Intravenous diltiazem infusion
Intravenous nitroglycerin infusion
Intravenous sodium nitroprusside infusion
Oral ramipril

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that Type B dissection is usually managed medically in the absence of spinal/mesenteric/limb malperfusion syndrome, with acute therapy consisting of intravenous antihypertensives titrated to a systolic BP of 120 mmHg measured by arterial line and a heart rate below 70 bpm in a critical care setting. The first-line agent is a combined alpha and beta-blocker such as labetalol, which lowers blood pressure and decreases cardiac contractility. This patient has an uncomplicated Type B dissection, so IV labetalol is the initial treatment and oral medications can follow after initial control.

optionExplanations.b: A nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem is used only when there are clear contraindications to beta-blockers, or as second-line therapy.
optionExplanations.c: IV nitroglycerin is listed as a second-line agent, not the initial choice for acute rate and pressure control.
optionExplanations.d: Vasodilators are added only if blood pressure or heart rate control is insufficient after alpha and beta-blockade, so they are not the initial agent.
optionExplanations.e: An ACEI is reserved for insufficient BP or HR control, and oral medications are used only after initial intravenous control is achieved.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman reports two years of progressive right leg swelling that no longer settles with elevation. The skin of the foot and ankle is thickened and hyperkeratotic, the edema does not pit, and the examiner is unable to lift a fold of skin at the base of the second toe. She has had two episodes of cellulitis in that limb. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Lymphoscintigraphy
Venous duplex ultrasound of the leg
Ankle-brachial index measurement
Punch biopsy of the thickened skin
CT venography of the pelvis

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes gives lymphoscintigraphy as the most definitive test for lymphedema, with secondary causes evaluated and treated if found. The classic features here are non-pitting edema with hyperkeratotic cutaneous changes on a limb with progressive disease and a positive Stemmer sign, the sensitive finding in which the examiner is unable to lift the skin of a thickened skin fold at the base of the second toe. Confirming impaired lymphatic drainage therefore requires lymphoscintigraphy rather than a study of the venous or arterial circulation.

optionExplanations.b: Duplex assesses venous reflux and obstruction, but the non-pitting edema, hyperkeratosis and positive Stemmer sign point to the lymphatics, not chronic venous insufficiency.
optionExplanations.c: The ankle-brachial index screens for arterial occlusive disease; it says nothing about lymphatic drainage and this limb has no ischemic features.
optionExplanations.d: Skin biopsy documents the hyperkeratotic cutaneous changes and lipodermatosclerosis already evident on examination and does not establish the lymphatic defect.
optionExplanations.e: Pelvic cross-sectional imaging is aimed at secondary causes such as pelvic tumours; it is pursued after the diagnosis is established rather than as the definitive test.

source.reference: VS12 — Lymphedema, Clinical Features and Investigations
